en: Thus have I heard: the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the Eighth in the Dīgha Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruññā in the Kaṇṇakatthala Deer Park.
Then the naked ascetic Kassapa approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Master Gotama:
‘The ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity; he single-mindedly censures and reviles every ascetic who lives a life of hardship.
Those, Master Gotama, who speak thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity...’”
‘One who lives a harsh life is entirely censured and reviled,’ do they speak as they were told by Master Gotama?
Do they not misrepresent Master Gotama with what is false? Do they explain in accordance with the Dhamma?
And does no legitimate criticism or ground for reproach arise against them?
"For we do not wish to misrepresent you, Master Gotama.
"Kassapa, those who say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity;
he single-mindedly reviles and censures every ascetic who lives a life of hardship'—they do not speak my words; they misrepresent me."
"Yet they have slandered me with what is untrue and false.

Here, Kassapa, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see certain ascetics of austere livelihood who, upon the dissolution of the body after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.

And here, Kassapa, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see certain ascetics of austere livelihood who, upon the dissolution of the body after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world."

Here, Kassapa, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see a certain ascetic living in comfort who, with the breakup of the body, after death, has reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

And here, Kassapa, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see another certain ascetic living in comfort who, with the breakup of the body, after death, has reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Kassapa, since I understand, as they really are, the coming and going, the passing away and rebirth of these ascetics,
why would I disparage all austerity, or why would I single-mindedly revile and reproach every ascetic who lives a life of austerity?

“Kassapa, there are some recluses and brahmins who are wise, clever, skilled in the doctrines of others, and as sharp as a hair-splitter. They move about as if piercing through views with the sword of wisdom.
In some respects my views agree with theirs, and in some respects they do not.
That which they say in some cases is ‘excellent,’ I too say in those same cases is ‘excellent.’”
That which some among them say is "not good," we too might say that some of it is "not good.
That which some among them say is "good," we might say that some of it is "not good.
And that which some among them say is "not good," we might say that some of it is "good."
That which we say is "good," others also say is "good.
That which we say is "not good," others also say is "not good.
That which we say is "not good," others say is "good."
That which we say is "good," others say is "not good.
1. Discourse on Cross-Examination:
Having approached them, I speak to them thus:
“Friends, as for those points on which we do not agree, let those points stand aside.
As for those points on which we do agree, regarding them a wise person—when investigating, scrutinizing, and examining them—would say of the Teacher or of the Saṅgha:

‘Those qualities of these venerable ones which are unwholesome, reckoned as unwholesome; blameworthy, reckoned as blameworthy; not to be cultivated, reckoned as not to be cultivated; unbefitting of an Ariyan, reckoned as unbefitting of an Ariyan; dark, reckoned as dark.’”
"Who is it that lives having abandoned these things without remainder—the recluse Gotama, or rather those other venerable teachers of groups?
"It is possible, Kassapa, that wise men, when investigating, scrutinizing, and examining the matter, might say:

'Those things of these venerable ones which are unwholesome, reckoned as unwholesome; blameworthy, reckoned as blameworthy; not to be cultivated, reckoned as not to be cultivated; unworthy of the noble ones, reckoned as unworthy of the noble ones; dark, reckoned as dark.'"
"The ascetic Gotama conducts himself having abandoned these things without remainder, whereas those worthy ones, the teachers of other schools, do not.
Thus, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and interrogate us on this matter, they would for the most part praise us alone.
Furthermore, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and interrogate our teacher as being the Teacher, or the Saṅgha as being the Saṅgha:

‘Of these things that are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome; blameless, reckoned as blameless; to be cultivated, reckoned as to be cultivated; noble, reckoned as noble; bright, reckoned as bright—who among these venerable ones practices them in their entirety:
is it the ascetic Gotama, or rather those other venerable teachers of groups?

Now it is possible, Kassapa, that wise people, when investigating, scrutinizing, and examining, might say this: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the text regarding the possibility of such a conclusion being reached based on the conduct of the respective teachers.*
‘Those qualities of these venerable ones which are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome; blameless, reckoned as blameless; to be cultivated, reckoned as to be cultivated; noble, reckoned as noble;
bright, reckoned as bright—the ascetic Gotama practices by undertaking them all without exception, whereas those other venerable teachers of groups [do not].
Thus, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and scrutinize the matter, they would for the most part praise us alone in that regard.
Furthermore, Kassapa, when an intelligent person investigates, probes, and interrogates us regarding the Teacher or the Saṅgha:

"Of these things which are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome, blameworthy and reckoned as blameworthy, not to be cultivated and reckoned as not to be cultivated, unworthy of the noble ones and reckoned as unworthy of the noble ones, dark and reckoned as dark—who among them acts having abandoned them without remainder:
the Saṅgha of Gotama’s disciples, or the Saṅghas of the disciples of other venerable teachers?"
"It is indeed possible, Kassapa, that wise people, when investigating, scrutinizing, and interrogating, might say this:

'Those qualities which these venerable ones consider unwholesome, considered as unwholesome; blameworthy, considered as blameworthy; not to be cultivated, considered as not to be cultivated; unworthy of the noble ones, considered as unworthy of the noble ones;

dark, considered as dark—the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples lives having abandoned these qualities without remainder, whereas the Saṅghas of the disciples of other teachers whom you honor do not.'"
"In this way, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and scrutinize us, they would for the most part praise us alone.
Furthermore, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and scrutinize our teacher or our teacher’s teacher, or our Saṅgha or our Saṅgha’s Saṅgha, [they would say]:

'Those qualities of these venerable ones which are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome; blameless, reckoned as blameless; to be cultivated, reckoned as to be cultivated; fit for an Ariya, reckoned as fit for an Ariya; bright, reckoned as bright—'"
"Who practices these teachings in their entirety: the community of disciples of Gotama, or rather, the venerable communities of teachers and disciples of other sects?
"It is possible, Kassapa, that when wise people investigate, examine, and scrutinize this, they would say:

'Those teachings of these venerable ones which are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome; blameless, reckoned as blameless; to be cultivated, reckoned as to be cultivated; noble, reckoned as noble; bright, reckoned as bright.'"
"The Saṅgha of the disciples of Gotama proceeds by undertaking these qualities without exception, whereas the venerable ones, the other teachers of groups, do not.
Thus, Kassapa, when wise people investigate, examine, and scrutinize this matter, they would for the most part praise us alone therein.
2. The Noble Eightfold Path.
"There is, Kassapa, a path, there is a way, by practicing which one will personally know and personally see:
'The ascetic Gotama alone speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
And what, Kassapa, is that path, what is that way, by practicing which one will personally know and personally see this?"
‘Is the ascetic Gotama one who speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks on the beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya?
It is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path.
That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

“This, Kassapa, is the path, this is the way, by practicing which one will personally know and personally see: ‘The ascetic Gotama alone speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Friend Gotama, these too are the ascetic practices of those recluses and brahmins that are reckoned as asceticism and reckoned as brahminhood. One is naked, rejecting conventions, licking one’s hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; one does not accept food brought or food specially prepared, nor an invitation. One does not accept food from the mouth of a pot, nor from the mouth of a basket, nor across a threshold, nor across a stick, nor across a pestle, nor from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing a child, nor from a woman living with a man, nor from where food is advertised to be distributed, nor from where a dog is waiting, nor from where flies are buzzing. One accepts no fish or meat, drinks no liquor, wine, or fermented brew. One keeps to one house, to one morsel; one keeps to two houses, to two morsels; ... [and so on] ... one keeps to seven houses, to seven morsels. One lives on one saucerful a day, on two saucerfuls a day, ... [and so on] ... on seven saucerfuls a day. One takes food once a day, once every two days, ... [and so on] ... once every seven days, or even longer. Thus one dwells pursuing the practice of eating at stated intervals. One is an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-parings, or moss, or rice-bran, or rice-scum, or sesamum flour, or grass, or cow dung. One lives on forest roots and fruits, one eats fallen fruits. One dresses in hemp, in hemp-mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in strips of antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood-shavings fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings.

One is a bird-feather wearer, one wears a garment of netting, one wears the skin of a living tiger, or a leopard, or a panther. One tears out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of tearing out hair and beard. One stands continuously, rejecting seats. One squats continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position. One uses a mattress of spikes; having made a mattress of spikes, he lies down on it. One dwells in what is agreed upon as a ‘bed-in-waiting,’ seeking the thrill of solitude. One dwells at the root of a tree, even during the rainy season. One dwells in an open, unsheltered place. One dwells wherever a night falls. One dwells in a charnel ground. One dwells in whatever abode is assigned by the Sangha. One wears a garment of felt, one wears an inner and outer robe, one wears a single inner and outer robe. One goes for alms in a single house, and having obtained alms there, one returns. One goes for alms only in the bowl, and having obtained alms in the bowl, one returns.

One eats only what is in the bowl, one eats sitting down, one does not eat more than one has eaten while sitting down. One refuses all further food. One is a drinker of water, one is an eater of greens. One is a one-session eater, one is a refuser of a second serving. One is a forest-dweller, one dwells in the forest. One is a refuse-rag wearer, one wears only refuse rags. One is a triple-robe wearer, one wears only three robes. One is a goer-for-alms, one depends solely on alms for sustenance. One is a house-to-house seeker, one passes directly by houses where no alms are given. One eats out of one vessel, one has only one vessel. One is a rinsing-water drinker, one is a rainwater drinker. One is a filterer of water, one is a drinker of filtered water. One dwells observing the arising and passing away of the body.”

He does not eat with a staff between his hands, nor with a pestle between them; he does not eat while two people are eating together; he does not eat from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in her courses;
he does not eat in crowds, nor where a dog is waiting, nor where flies are swarming;
he does not drink fish, meat, liquor, spirits, or grain-beer.
Thus, he either frequents a single house and takes a single morsel of food, or he frequents two houses and takes two morsels of food… or he frequents seven houses and takes seven morsels of food;
he subsists on one alms-offering, or he subsists on two alms-offerings… or he subsists on as many as seven alms-offerings;

he takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days… or he takes food once every seven days. In this way, he dwells engaged in the practice of taking meals at intervals, even up to once every half-month.
"Friend Gotama, these ascetic practices of those recluses and brahmins are indeed reckoned as 'recluseship' and 'brahminhood.
One eats only greens, or one eats millet, or one eats wild rice, or one eats horse-gram,
or one eats water-weeds, or one eats rice-powder, or one eats the scum of boiled rice, or one eats oil-cake..."
Or he eats grass, or he eats cow dung, or he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only what ripens naturally.
These, friend Gotama, are the ascetic practices of these recluses and brahmins that are reckoned as "recluseship" and "brahminhood.
He wears hempen clothes, or he wears hemp-mixed clothes, or he wears shrouds from corpses, or he wears rag-robes.
He wears garments made of tirīṭa grass; he wears an antelope skin; he wears a cloak made of pieces of antelope skin;
he wears a garment of kusa grass; he wears a garment of bark; he wears a garment of wood-shavings; he wears a blanket of human hair; he wears a blanket of animal wool;
he wears a cloak of owl feathers.
He is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard;
he is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats;
he is one who squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting.
He is one who uses a bed of thorns; he makes his bed on a bed of thorns,
he makes his bed on a plank, he makes his bed on the bare ground,
and he is one who sleeps on one side.
Wearing dust and dirt,
he dwells in the open air and accepts whatever seat is offered.
“He is one who goes naked, devoted to the practice of eating disgusting food;
he is one who abstains from drinking, devoted to the practice of non-drinking;
he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day, including the evening.”

4. Discourse on the Futility of Undertaking Austerities “Kassapa, even if one is naked, follows no conventional rules of conduct, scratches the ground with one’s hand... [and so on]... and dwells devoted to the practice of eating food at intervals of half a month;

yet if this perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, and perfection of wisdom have not been developed and realized by him, then he is far indeed from the state of a recluse and far indeed from the state of a brahmin.”
But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will, and through the destruction of the taints,
dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
then, Kassapa, such a bhikkhu is called a recluse as well as a brahmin.
If, Kassapa, one subsists on eating only sākā greens, or on eating millet, or indeed lives on forest roots and fruits, subsisting on whatever fruit has fallen;
yet if this perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, and perfection of wisdom have not been developed and realized by him,
then he is far indeed from the state of a recluse and far indeed from the state of a brahmin.
But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will, and through the destruction of the taints,
dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
then, Kassapa, such a bhikkhu is called a recluse as well as a brahmin.
Even if, Kassapa, he wears hempen robes, or even wears robes made of bark-fiber …pe… or dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water up to the third time each day;
yet this perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, and perfection of wisdom have not been developed and realized by him.
Then he is indeed far from the state of a recluse and far from the state of a brahmin.
But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will,

and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, he enters upon and dwells in it.
“This, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse and also a brahmin.
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One:
“Difficult, Master Gotama, is the state of a recluse; difficult is the state of a brahmin.”
“Kassapa, it is indeed the nature of things in the world that ‘the state of a recluse is difficult to practice, the state of a brahmin is difficult to practice.
Kassapa, suppose one is naked, disregarding conventions, licking one’s hands... [and so on]... and dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even once every half-month.

Yet, Kassapa, if by this measure or by this exertion of asceticism the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin were difficult to practice, extremely difficult to practice, then it would not be right to say:”
‘The life of a recluse is difficult to practice; the life of a brahmin is difficult to practice.
Yet it would be possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even a slave-girl with a water-jar to do this:

‘Come now, let me become one who goes naked, who observes no conventions of conduct, who cleanses himself with his hands... [and so on]... thus I shall dwell devoted to the practice of eating food according to a fixed sequence only once every half-month.’”

But because, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this practice of austerity, the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin is difficult to achieve, very difficult to achieve, therefore it is right to say:
"The state of a recluse is difficult; the state of a brahmin is difficult.
And when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will, and through the destruction of the taints...
Having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he enters and dwells therein.
This, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse and also a brahmin.
Even if, Kassapa, he subsists on greens, or on millet, or—even as far as—he lives sustained by forest roots and fruits, eating only fallen fruit.
"Kassapa, if asceticism or brahminhood were difficult to achieve, very difficult to achieve, by this measure and by this practice of austerity, it would not be right to say:
'Asceticism is difficult; brahminhood is difficult.
For it would be possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even for a slave girl with a water-jar to accomplish it."
‘Come now, let me subsist on greens, or on millet... [and so on] ...or let me maintain myself by eating forest roots and fruits, living on fallen fruit.

But since, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this practice of austerity, the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin is difficult to achieve, very difficult to achieve, it is therefore appropriate to say:
‘The state of a recluse is difficult to achieve; the state of a brahmin is difficult to achieve.’”
But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will,
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells therein—
this, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse and also a brahmin.
“Even if, Kassapa, he wears hempen garments, or even wears garments of bark-fiber … [and so on] … he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water up to the third time each day.

Yet, Kassapa, if by this measure or by this undertaking of asceticism the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin were difficult to achieve, very difficult to achieve, it would not be right to say:
‘The state of a recluse is difficult; the state of a brahmin is difficult.’”
Moreover, Kassapa, it would have been possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even a slave-girl with a water-jar to say:
"Come now, I shall wear hempen garments; I shall wear garments of hemp-mixed cloth... and I shall dwell devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day.

But since, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this ascetic practice, the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin is difficult to achieve, very difficult to achieve, therefore it is appropriate to say this: [that such asceticism is necessary].
“It is difficult to practice the life of a recluse; it is difficult to practice the life of a brahmin.

But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity and free from ill will—and, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon them.
“This, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse indeed and a brahmin indeed.
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One:
“It is difficult to recognize a recluse, Master Gotama; it is difficult to recognize a brahmin.”
“Kassapa, it is indeed the nature of things in the world that ‘a recluse is hard to recognize, a brahmin is hard to recognize.
Even if, Kassapa, one is naked, follows no fixed rules of conduct, scratches the ground with his hand... [and so on] ...and lives devoted to the practice of taking food at intervals of half a month;
yet, Kassapa, by this measure alone or by this mere exertion of austerity, a recluse or a brahmin would still be hard to recognize, very hard to recognize, and it would not be right to say:”
“It is difficult to know a recluse, difficult to know a brahmin.
Yet it would be possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even for a slave-girl with a water-jar, to know him thus:
“This man is a naked ascetic, one who lives in the open air, one who scrapes his hands clean... [and so on] ... he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals of half a month.”

But because, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this practice of austerity, it is difficult to recognize, very difficult to recognize, whether one is a recluse or a brahmin, therefore it is appropriate to say:
‘A recluse is difficult to recognize; a brahmin is difficult to recognize.
For when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity and free from ill will—and through the destruction of the taints...
Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he enters and dwells therein.
This, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse and also a brahmin.
Even if, Kassapa, he subsists on greens, on millet... [and so on] ...or lives sustained by forest roots and fruits, eating only fallen fruit.
"Kassapa, by this much and by this practice of austerity, it would not have been difficult or very difficult to recognize whether one was an ascetic or a brahmin;
it would not have been right to say, 'An ascetic is difficult to recognize, a brahmin is difficult to recognize.
Indeed, it would have been possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even for a slave girl with a water-jar, to know him."
‘He eats only vegetables, or he eats only wild millet... [and so on] ...he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only windfallen fruit.

But because, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this practice of austerity, it is difficult, indeed very difficult, to recognize whether one is a recluse or a brahmin, therefore it is appropriate to say:
‘A recluse is difficult to recognize; a brahmin is difficult to recognize.’”
But when, Kassapa, a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness that is free from enmity and free from ill will,
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells therein—
this, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse and also a brahmin.

“Kassapa, even if one wears hempen robes, or wears robes made of bark-fiber … [and so on] … or dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water up to the third time each day—even by this measure and by this undertaking of asceticism, Kassapa, a recluse or a brahmin would not be difficult to recognize, nor very difficult to recognize; it would not be right to say:
‘A recluse is difficult to recognize, a brahmin is difficult to recognize.’”
Moreover, it would have been possible for a householder, or a householder’s son, or even a slave-girl with a water-pot to know:
“This person wears hempen garments, he wears garments of bark-fiber... he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water up to three times a day.

But because, Kassapa, apart from this measure and apart from this ascetic exertion, it is difficult, very difficult to recognize whether one is a recluse or a brahmin, therefore it is appropriate to say this: [that true asceticism lies elsewhere].
“It is difficult to know a recluse, it is difficult to know a brahmin. Kassapa,
when a bhikkhu develops a mind of loving-kindness— free from enmity and free from ill will— and, through the destruction of the taints,
dwells having personally realized and attained in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he is indeed difficult to know.
“This, Kassapa, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse as well as a brahmin.

When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One: [5. The Perfection of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom] When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“But what, Master Gotama, is that accomplishment in virtue, what is that accomplishment in mind, and what is that accomplishment in wisdom?

“Here, Kassapa, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One … [as in the standard formula] … seeing danger in the slightest fault, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training; he is endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, pure in livelihood, accomplished in virtue, guarded in the doors of the sense faculties, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and contented. This, Kassapa, is called accomplishment in virtue.”
And how, Kassapa, is a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue?

Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
This, too, is his accomplishment in virtue... [and so on]...
Or again, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, maintain their lives by such low arts and wrong livelihood as these:
rites for propitiating deities, rites of incantation, ... [and so on] ... the recitation of charms over medicinal herbs.
He abstains from such low arts and wrong livelihood.
This too belongs to his perfection of virtue.
Kassapa, a bhikkhu who is thus perfected in virtue perceives no fear from anywhere, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Just as, Kassapa, a consecrated khattiya king who has defeated his enemies perceives no fear from anywhere, namely, from his adversaries; so it is with him.
In the same way, Kassapa, a bhikkhu who is thus perfected in virtue perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
It is in this way, Kassapa, that a bhikkhu is perfected in virtue.
This, Kassapa, is the perfection of virtue...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This, too, is his perfection of mind... [as before] ...
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
This too belongs to his perfection of mind.
This, Kassapa, is the perfection of mind.
When his mind is thus concentrated... [pe]...
He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision;
this too is his perfection of wisdom...
[and so on] ...he understands: "There is nothing further beyond this state of being."
This too belongs to his perfection of wisdom.
This, Kassapa, is the perfection of wisdom.

And, Kassapa, there is no other perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, or perfection of wisdom that is higher or more sublime than this perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, and perfection of wisdom.
6. Discourse on the Lion’s Roar:
“Kassapa, there are some ascetics and brahmins who advocate for virtue;
they speak in many ways in praise of virtue.”
"To whatever extent, Kassapa, there is noble, supreme virtue, I do not see anyone who is my equal therein, much less superior.
Indeed, I alone am superior therein, namely, in regard to higher virtue.
There are, Kassapa, some recluses and brahmins who advocate austerity and self-disgust."
They praise asceticism and self-disgust in many ways.
Kassapa, as far as the supreme asceticism and self-disgust of the noble ones extends, I do not see anyone who is my equal therein, much less superior.
On the contrary, I alone am superior therein, namely, in regard to self-disgust.
“Kassapa, there are some recluses and brahmins who profess wisdom;
they speak in many ways in praise of wisdom.
However, Kassapa, as for the supreme noble wisdom, I do not see anyone who is my equal therein, let alone superior.”
But I am even more so in that regard, namely, in terms of higher wisdom.
Kassapa, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim liberation;
they speak in many ways in praise of liberation.
"To whatever extent, Kassapa, there is noble supreme liberation, I do not see anyone who is my equal therein, much less superior.
Indeed, I alone am superior therein, namely, by way of higher liberation.
However, Kassapa, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this:"
“The ascetic Gotama roars the lion’s roar, but he roars it only in empty places, not in assemblies.
To them, Kassapa, you should say: “Do not speak thus.
You should rather say: ‘The ascetic Gotama roars the lion’s roar, and he roars it in assemblies.’”
"It is possible, Kassapa, that wanderers of other sects might say:
'The ascetic Gotama roars his lion's roar, and he roars in assemblies, yet he does not roar with confidence.
To them, you should say: 'Do not say so!'"
‘The ascetic Gotama roars his lion’s roar, and he roars it in assemblies, and he roars it with confidence’—this, Kassapa, is what you should say.
But it is possible, Kassapa, that wanderers of other sects might say this:
‘The ascetic Gotama roars his lion’s roar, and he roars it in assemblies, and he roars it with confidence, yet they do not question him... [and so on].”
They ask him questions, yet when questioned, he does not answer their questions... [and so on]...
he answers their questions, yet he does not satisfy their minds with his explanations of those questions... [and so on]...
he satisfies their minds with his explanations of those questions, yet they do not think it worth listening to... [and so on].
They think they should listen to him; yet having listened, they do not gain confidence.
… Having listened, they gain confidence; yet they do not manifest an attitude of confidence. … They manifest an attitude of confidence;
yet they do not practice in accordance with that state. … [and so on] …
‘They practice for suchness, yet those who have practiced do not achieve success.
To them, it should be said: ‘Do not say so!
The ascetic Gotama roars the lion’s roar; he roars in assemblies; he roars with confidence; and regarding a question—’
“They ask him questions, and when questioned, he answers them; by his answering of questions, he satisfies their minds.
They think they should listen to him, and having listened, they gain confidence; they manifest that confidence and practice accordingly;
and practicing thus, they attain fulfillment. It is in this way, Kassapa, that you should speak.
7. Discussion on the Probationary Period for Heretics Once, Kassapa, I was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There, a certain ascetic practitioner of the holy life named Nigrodha asked me a question regarding self-loathing.
“Being asked a question regarding higher refinement, I answered him.
And when I had answered, he was satisfied with me as if he were intoxicated.
“Who indeed, venerable sir, would not be satisfied with the Blessed One’s Dhamma upon hearing it, as if they were intoxicated?”
"Indeed, Bhante, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, I am as delighted as if I were intoxicated.
Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or as one might show the way to one who has lost his path, or as one might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the full ordination.
“Kassapa, whoever was formerly a member of another sect who desires the going-forth and desires the full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya must undergo a four-month probation.
At the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with him, they grant him the going-forth and the full ordination.”
“They give them the going-forth and ordain them for the state of a monk.
Moreover, I recognize a distinction between individuals in this matter.
“Venerable sir, if those who were formerly members of other sects desire the going-forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, they desire it...”

“They undergo probation for four months; at the end of those four months, the monks—being satisfied with them—grant them the going-forth and ordain them into the state of a monk. I shall undergo probation for four years;
at the end of those four years, may the monks—being satisfied with me—grant me the going-forth and ordain me into the state of a monk.”
The naked ascetic Kassapa received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Not long after his ordination, the Venerable Kassapa, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein. He declared:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus the Venerable Kassapa became one of the Arahants.
The Mahāsīhanādasutta, the eighth, is finished.
